subsequent

/SUB-si-kwent/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something that is subsequent is coming after something in time.

The subsequent chapters explained what happened after the storm.

Example

A novelist's first book sells barely a hundred copies. Yet each subsequent book she publishes earns better reviews and a larger audience, until the fifth one becomes a bestseller.

Her later books are defined by coming after that first flop in time, which is exactly the relationship subsequent describes. Subsequent is more precise than 'later' because it explicitly ties the following events to a specific earlier one in a sequence.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

following: Following means coming immediately after something — the following day, the following chapter, with nothing in between. Subsequent is looser about distance: a subsequent chapter may come next or much further on. It promises only that it comes after that particular earlier point, near or far.

succeeding: Succeeding means coming next in a fixed series, each item taking the previous one's place — succeeding kings, succeeding editions. Subsequent does not need a series at all: anything that happens after a particular earlier event is subsequent to it, whether or not it belongs to the same line.

resulting: Resulting describes what an earlier event caused — the storm and the resulting damage. Subsequent claims only order in time: a subsequent meeting comes after the first one whether or not the first caused it. Every resulting event is subsequent, but a subsequent event may be entirely unconnected.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

previous: coming before something else in time

prior: existing or happening earlier than something

Where it sits · how tightly it follows what happened

eventual → later → subsequent → ensuing

eventual vs. subsequent: Eventual is vaguer and weaker than subsequent — an eventual result happens at some unknown future point, while a subsequent one clearly comes after a specific event.

later vs. subsequent: Later is weaker than subsequent; later just means afterward at some point, but subsequent points to what came after a particular event, often in order.

ensuing vs. subsequent: Ensuing is stronger than subsequent — subsequent events simply come after, while ensuing events follow immediately and often as a direct result.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — sub-: under; close after (Latin)

root — sequ: to follow (Latin (sequi))

suffix — -ent: in a state or condition of (Latin)

Put it together: Sub- (close after) + sequ (follow) + -ent: subsequent describes what follows close behind — coming after something else in time.

Use the root in a new word: sequel: Fans lined up at midnight for the first showing of the sequel.

Root Check

Word Choice

Subsequent has a slightly formal, narrative register, fitting naturally into writing that lays out a sequence of events (subsequent chapters, subsequent investigations) better than everyday speech.
